name: The Veblen Good
statement: A luxury wanted more precisely because it costs more, since the high price is the point.
statementAccent: wanted more precisely because it costs more
meaning: A Veblen good is a luxury or status good for which demand increases as its price increases, in apparent contradiction of the law of demand. A higher price makes the good more desirable, because its expense and exclusivity signal wealth and prestige, so raising the price can raise demand over some range, giving it an upward-sloping demand curve. The idea descends from the economist and sociologist Thorstein Veblen, who introduced the concept of conspicuous consumption in his 1899 book The Theory of the Leisure Class, arguing that the wealthy display their status through visibly expensive consumption. The terms Veblen good and Veblen effect were coined later by Harvey Leibenstein in a 1950 paper that distinguished the Veblen effect from the related snob and bandwagon effects. Luxury cars, fine champagne, designer goods, and prestige watches are typical examples: their appeal depends partly on being costly and exclusive.
mechanism: For an ordinary good, demand falls as price rises. A Veblen good works differently because part of its value lies in what its price signals. The good is desired as a marker of status and wealth, so a high price and the exclusivity it enforces are not deterrents but attractions: they advertise that the owner can afford what others cannot. Lowering the price would undermine this appeal by making the good more affordable and therefore less exclusive and prestigious, so demand can actually fall. This is a preference-price interaction, in which the price itself enters the buyer's valuation as a signal. Leibenstein set the Veblen effect alongside two companions: the snob effect, where demand for a good falls as more people own it because consumers seek exclusivity, and the bandwagon effect, where demand rises as more people own it because consumers want to follow the crowd. Together these describe how the choices and status of others shape individual demand.

examples.text: Luxury watches and cars can sell better at higher prices, since the expense itself signals status and exclusivity that buyers value.
Veblen's idea that the wealthy display status through visibly costly consumption underlies the appeal of goods whose price is part of the point.
Lowering the price of a status good can reduce its appeal by making it less exclusive, so demand may fall rather than rise.

variants.name: The snob effect
variants.text: Leibenstein's related effect in which demand for a good falls as more people own it, because consumers desire exclusivity and differentiation.

variants.name: The bandwagon effect
variants.text: Leibenstein's related effect in which demand for a good rises as more people own it, because consumers want to follow others.

whyItMatters: The Veblen good is an important concept in the economics of luxury, marketing, and status or positional goods, and a notable exception to the law of demand. It captures how, for some goods, price is not merely a cost but a signal, so that expense and exclusivity are precisely what make the good desirable, reshaping how firms price and position luxury products. Rooted in Veblen's analysis of conspicuous consumption and formalised through Leibenstein's distinction of the Veblen, snob, and bandwagon effects, the idea connects economics to sociology and to the study of how people use consumption to display and pursue status. It explains behaviour that a naive demand model misses, from premium pricing strategies to the paradox that cutting a luxury's price can diminish its allure, making it central to understanding markets where prestige, not just utility, drives demand.

working.text: recognise that for a status good, a high price advertises wealth and exclusivity, entering the buyer's valuation as a signal.
note that a higher price can increase the good's prestige and desirability, so demand rises over some range.
see that lowering the price can reduce exclusivity and appeal, so demand may fall, unlike an ordinary good.

limits: The Veblen effect operates only over a range and only for goods valued as status symbols; beyond some point, or for ordinary goods, the usual law of demand reasserts itself, so upward-sloping demand is not unlimited. The effect depends on the price and consumption being visible and socially meaningful, so it applies to conspicuous luxuries rather than private necessities. It coexists with the opposing snob and bandwagon effects, so the net influence of others' choices on demand can be complex. And distinguishing genuine Veblen behaviour from ordinary quality signalling, where higher price reliably indicates better goods, can be difficult in practice. So the Veblen good is a real and important exception confined to status-driven luxury markets rather than a general reversal of the law of demand.
misreadings: A Veblen good is not the same as a Giffen good; both can show demand rising with price, but a Veblen good is a luxury desired for status, while a Giffen good is an inferior staple driven by the income effect. The effect does not mean any price rise always increases demand; it holds only over a range and only for goods whose price signals prestige. And it is not merely that expensive things are better; the point is that the expense itself confers desirability through exclusivity, so treating all higher-priced goods as Veblen goods, or the effect as unbounded, misreads a phenomenon specific to conspicuous, status-laden consumption.
origin: Descended from Thorstein Veblen's concept of conspicuous consumption in his 1899 book The Theory of the Leisure Class, with the terms Veblen good and Veblen effect coined by Harvey Leibenstein in a 1950 paper alongside the snob and bandwagon effects.
